title: Delete Duplicate Folders in System
statement:
`paths` describes a tree of folders: each `paths[i]` lists the folder names on the way from the top of the file system down to one folder, so `["one", "two", "three"]` stands for `/one/two/three`. Every folder is listed exactly once, and the parent of every folder below the top level is listed too.

Call two different folders **identical** when both have at least one subfolder and their contents match all the way down: they have the same set of subfolder names, and the subfolders with the same name have matching contents in turn (two empty subfolders with the same name match). The two folders' own names, depths and positions do not matter.

- Every folder that is identical to at least one other folder is marked, together with everything inside it.
- All marked folders are then deleted in one pass. Folders that only become identical after this deletion are kept.

Return the paths of the folders that remain, in any order.
constraints: paths[i][j] contains only lowercase English letters
No two paths name the same folder
The parent of every folder below the top level is also in paths
notes:
## Intuition

The paths describe a tree, so first rebuild it as a trie: one node per folder, children keyed by name. Two folders are identical exactly when the shapes below them are equal, names included. Comparing every pair of folders subtree by subtree works but is far too slow on big trees. Instead, give each folder a **canonical string** for its contents, built bottom-up: each child contributes `name(childString)`, and the pieces are sorted so the order the paths arrived in does not matter. Equal contents give equal strings, so one hash map of string counts finds every duplicate.

## Approach

1. Insert every path into a trie rooted at `root`; each node has `children` (a `Map`) and a `key`.
2. `serialize` each node after its children: a leaf returns `''`; otherwise collect `name(childKey)` for each child, sort, join, store it in `node.key` and add one to `counts` for that key.
3. Walk the trie again with `collect`. Skip a child whose key is non-empty and appears more than once: it is deleted along with its whole subtree. Otherwise record its path from `current` and descend.
4. Return `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

Folders `/a/b`, `/c/b` and `/d/a` are leaves, so their keys are `''`. Then `/a` gets key `b()`, `/c` gets `b()` and `/d` gets `a()`, so `counts` maps `b()` to 2 and `a()` to 1. In `collect`, `/a` and `/c` are skipped (their key appears twice), and `/d` survives along with `/d/a`, giving `[["d"], ["d","a"]]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(S log S), where S is the number of characters in `paths`. Each name is copied into the key of every ancestor, and there are exactly as many ancestor–descendant pairs as names in all the paths, so all keys together are O(S) long; sorting the pieces adds the log factor.
- Space: O(S) for the trie and its keys.

## Pitfalls

- Leaves are never identical to each other (they have no subfolders), so an empty key must never count as a duplicate.
- Sort the children's pieces; insertion order differs between equal folders.
- Wrap each child's string in brackets; plain concatenation would let different trees produce the same string.
- Delete once: decide from the original tree, not after removing folders.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `root` | trie node above the top-level folders |
| `node.children` | map from a subfolder's name to its node |
| `node.key` | canonical string of the folder's contents (`''` for a leaf) |
| `counts` | how many folders have each key |
| `parts` | the `name(childKey)` pieces of one folder |
| `current` | path of names to the folder being visited |
| `result` | paths of the folders that remain |
